title: realloc, resizing and preserving the original allocation on failure
learningObjectives: Explain the concept and its C rules.
Trace the example and identify data or resource flow.
Recognize relevant safety and failure cases.
Apply the concept in a tested C program.

understand.concept: realloc attempts to resize an allocated block while preserving the contents up to the smaller of the old and new sizes. On failure for a nonzero requested size, it returns NULL and the original allocation remains valid. Assigning directly to the only owning pointer can lose that allocation.
understand.whyItMatters: Safe resizing needs a temporary pointer so failure does not overwrite the original owner. The program must also define behaviour for zero requested size according to the C version and library contract it targets.
understand.analogy: Treat each object or stream as a resource with a defined lifetime and explicit rules for access.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not replace C's formal object, storage-duration, alignment or library rules.

explain.narrative:
realloc attempts to resize an allocated block while preserving the contents up to the smaller of the old and new sizes. On failure for a nonzero requested size, it returns NULL and the original allocation remains valid. Assigning directly to the only owning pointer can lose that allocation.

Check all allocation, I/O and conversion results. Respect object bounds and lifetime, initialize data before reading it, and define who owns and releases each resource.

examples.title: Focused C example
examples.explanation: grown receives the result. If realloc fails, items still owns the original block and can be freed. If it succeeds, the returned pointer becomes the new owner and is assigned back to items.

practise.guidedTask: Explain why assigning realloc directly to items is dangerous on failure.
practise.independentTask: Write a resize helper that checks multiplication overflow, preserves the old pointer on failure and updates the count only after success.
hints: After successful realloc, use the returned pointer; the old pointer may no longer be valid.
Do not access newly added bytes before initializing them.
Define an explicit policy for a requested size of zero.
